one_liner: Rust LZ/entropy codec with a C ABI whose blocks decode in parallel; mixed one-core result against zstd -3, wins multicore reads.
what_it_does: Glyd is a lossless compression library and CLI in Rust, exported to C/C++ through include/glyd.h (libglyd shared or static). Levels span an LZ4-class default/fast/turbo tier (format v6), a zstd -3-class --max and a zstd -19-class --ultra (format v9), and a context-mixing --cold tier, plus record mode (-r: logs, CSV, SQL dumps, JSON lines turned into typed columns) and base mode (--base: delta against a previous version). It is not API- or format-compatible with zstd or LZ4: you call glyd_compress*/glyd_decompress* (caller-buffer) or glyd_compress2/glyd_decompress2 (library-allocated, freed with glyd_free), and only Glyd can read the output.
how_it_is_fast: Input is cut into 256 KB blocks and, on the parallel paths, into independent units (one per core, up to 128 MB) so a single stream decodes on every core, which is where the 8-thread read numbers come from. The --max tier uses 8-way interleaved Huffman literals and tANS-coded sequences with repeat offsets over a double-fast parse with an 8 MB window, modeled on zstd's design; the default tier is an LZAV-class finder with a minimum match of 7 and copy-only decode loops. Match finding has an AVX2+BMI2 path chosen at run time and NEON decode/checksum paths on aarch64.
when_to_use: Write-once, read-many data (object storage, data lakes, release assets) where reads run on several cores per stream: Glyd's units decode in parallel while a zstd or LZ4 frame decodes on one thread.
Logs, CSV/TSV, SQL dumps and JSON lines where record mode (-r) stores 12-61% fewer bytes than zstd -3 per the README, if read CPU is not the bill.
Versioned blobs (nightly dumps, images, source tarballs) where --base stored 1.1-2.1x less than zstd --patch-from at the fast tier in the author's tests.
aarch64 servers (Graviton3) where the author's one-core --max decode was 1.10x zstd -3 at a slightly better ratio (3.98 vs 3.86).
when_not_to_use: Single-threaded decode on recent Intel x86: on Sapphire Rapids --max decoded at 1,287 MB/s vs zstd -3's 1,518 (0.85x), and the README's own known-gaps list gives 0.79-0.97x there.
Write-heavy workloads: --max compresses at 0.71-0.77x zstd -3's speed and default at about 0.66-0.72x LZ4's; record mode halves write speed again and reads cost 2-2.7x zstd's CPU.
Anything needing interoperability: the format is Glyd-only, with no other decoder; zstd and LZ4 frames are read everywhere.
Small objects with a dictionary: the README says sizes tie with zstd and zstd is 1.4-2x faster per object.

Risk-averse production use: a one-author project (240 stars, 1 fork, 0 issues filed) at v0.26.0 whose formats have already gone through v6-v9, and whose store and GPU parts are BUSL-1.1 (commercial use needs a license).

integration.form: crate (also cdylib/staticlib with C header include/glyd.h; prebuilt libraries per release)
integration.dependencies: none at run time for the core codec beyond Rust std; the default features pull glyd-preflate (vendored) and lepton_jpeg only to read v0.12-v0.13 container files (--no-default-features drops them); Rayon for the parallel paths
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.80+ (README badge); benchmarks built with rustc 1.98
integration.platforms: x86-64 (AVX2+BMI2 fast path, scalar fallback otherwise), aarch64 (NEON); release binaries for Linux x86_64, Linux aarch64, macOS arm64
integration.thread_safety: not documented for the C API; the source uses thread-local scratch tables and a process-wide thread count (glyd::set_threads, an atomic), and the *_parallel C functions run on Rayon's global pool across all cores
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it fills the same slot as zstd -3 / LZ4 but has its own API and an incompatible format; existing zstd/LZ4 data and readers cannot use it

gotchas: The 22.7 GB/s and 10.4 GB/s headline reads are 8-thread Glyd against single-thread zstd and LZ4 frame decoding; like for like on one core the gain over zstd -3 is 1.10x on Graviton3 and a loss on Sapphire Rapids.

The LZ4 baseline in examples/bench_suite.rs is the lz4 crate's frame encoder at level 1 and its streaming Decoder with read_to_end, not liblz4's block API, so LZ4 decode measured only about 1.2-1.4 GB/s; the default-vs-LZ4 decode gap is likely overstated.
Glyd verifies a CRC32C per block on decode while the zstd frames in the benchmark carry no checksum, which slightly favors zstd's decode numbers.

include/glyd.h comments still describe --max as format v7 while the README says v9; libglyd_store (BUSL-1.1) re-exports the whole codec API, so linking the wrong library silently changes your license terms.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Over Zstandard (zstd) when reads of large objects can use several cores and you control both ends of the format; stay with zstd for one-core decode on x86, faster writes and universal readers. Over LZ4 or lzvolt only if you want a better ratio with parallel decode; for the fastest single-thread block decode, LZ4's block API, lzvolt or ZXC are the better-measured choices.
verified_claims_summary: First-party suite of 2026-09-21 on an 8.7 GB corpus (logs, JSON events, SQL dumps, Parquet), rustc 1.98 with target-cpu=native and fat LTO, in-process libzstd 1.5.7 and the lz4 crate, on Graviton3 (c7g.2xlarge) and Xeon Platinum 8488C (c7i.2xlarge): one thread, --max decoded 1,571 vs zstd -3 1,425 MB/s on Graviton3 (1.10x) but 1,287 vs 1,518 on Sapphire Rapids (0.85x), and compressed slower on both (233 vs 313, 266 vs 377). Default decoded 3,309 and 2,752 MB/s vs LZ4 frame 1,394 and 1,206; the 8-thread figures compare parallel Glyd with single-thread zstd/LZ4 decoding.
status_note: Very actively developed (1,039 commits, last commit 2026-10-03, v0.26.0) by a single author; the codec is BSD-3-Clause OR GPL-2.0 and usable commercially, but it is young, has no external users visible in the issue tracker, and the store/GPU parts are BUSL-1.1.
